messages.content: Write the engineering culture section of a careers page. Around 250 words.

Assuming this is generic careers-page copy (no company details were given) — here it is, ready to swap in real numbers:

---

**How we build**

We ship small and often. Most changes go out the day they're written, and the average pull request here touches under 200 lines. If yours is bigger, someone will ask why before they ask anything else.

Nobody owns a file. Everybody owns the pager. Engineers carry a one-week on-call rotation for the systems they wrote, which turns 3 a.m. into a design constraint instead of somebody else's problem.

Code review is honest and fast. We would rather hear "this won't survive contact with the job queue" on Tuesday than read it in a postmortem in March. Disagreements get written down and then decided, usually by whoever sits closest to the code rather than whoever has the longest title.

We write. Design docs before the big work, postmortems after the outages, and both are readable by people outside the team. When an incident happens we go after the missing guardrail, not the person who tripped over it.

About a fifth of every quarter goes to work no customer asked for: the flaky test suite, the migration everyone has been stepping around, the tool that saves the support team an hour a day. Engineers pick that work themselves.

There is no hero culture here, and no one is measured on hours. We hire people who explain things clearly, change their minds when the data says so, and care whether the thing actually works for the person on the other end.

---

Word count: ~250. Tell me the company, stack, team size, or real on-call and review practices and I'll tighten it around those specifics.

output:
**How we build**

Small changes, shipped often. Most of what gets written goes out the same day, and a typical pull request here runs under 200 lines. Bring one that's a thousand lines long and someone will ask about the shape of it before they read a line.

Files have no owners. The pager has plenty. Whoever builds a system takes a week in its rotation, which turns 3 a.m. into something you design around instead of hand off.

Reviews come back fast and say what they mean. Better to hear on Tuesday that a change will fall over the first time the job queue gets busy than to find it in a postmortem next March. When people disagree, they write it down and somebody decides, usually the person nearest the code rather than the one with the longest title.

Writing matters here. Design docs go up before the large work starts, postmortems after things break, and both are meant to be legible to people outside the team. After an incident we look for the guardrail that was missing, and leave alone the engineer who walked past it.

Roughly a day a week goes to work nobody requested: the test suite that fails at random, the migration everyone routes around, the small tool that gives support an hour back. Engineers pick that work themselves.

No heroics, and nobody counts hours. We look for people who explain things well, who change their minds when the evidence turns, and who care whether the thing works for whoever ends up on the other side of it.
